become overly compliant when feeling threatened
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette: Manuel, a 70-year-old widowed welder from Latin America, sat in his cluttered living room, the shadows lengthening as evening approached. His hands, calloused from years of labor, trembled slightly as he recalled a time that haunted him. It was decades ago, during a tumultuous period of political unrest in his home country, when he was captured and tortured by government forces. The memories were not distant; they felt present, as if the terror was happening again in that very moment. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a car door slamming, a sudden shout from a neighbor — felt like warnings he couldn't afford to ignore, and he found himself bracing for danger in moments that should have felt safe. "Because the memory came back so vividly, he began to see threads of it everywhere: in the shadow of passing cars, in the way people raised their voices during arguments, and in the tension of the air before a storm." Gunshots, echoing in the distance, triggered visceral reactions in him that no amount of time could diminish. Each crack of a firearm sent waves of panic coursing through his body, transporting him back to the dark, oppressive room where he had been held. In moments of distress, Manuel found himself trapped in a cycle of detachment. He would often try to push the memories away, suppressing the thoughts of his past as if they were mere shadows. Yet, the harder he fought to forget, the more vivid the memories became, erupting into his consciousness with an intensity that left him gasping for air, filled with rage at his helplessness. He had come to believe that this rage, this intense feeling boiling within him, was an unending reminder of his failure to protect himself and others during that horrific time. The conclusion that he was powerless in the face of such trauma led him to withdraw further from those around him, believing that isolating himself was the only rational choice to avoid potential harm. The guilt gnawed at him, leading him to think that he could have done more, that perhaps if he had fought harder, he could have changed the course of those dark days. The self-blame became suffocating, reinforcing his fear of the world around him. He felt that he could never truly know who might betray or harm him again, and this belief made him overly compliant in interactions, as if by pleasing others, he could somehow stave off danger. The weight of his past loomed heavily over his present. Every time he heard the clanging of metal at the welding shop, he was reminded of his past traumas, which only confirmed his belief that the world was a dangerous place and that he had no control over his surroundings. When he ventured out to the welding shop, the sounds of machinery often morphed into echoes of his trauma, the clanging metal reminding him too much of the violence he had endured. His colleagues noticed his abrupt withdrawal, how he would flinch at loud noises and retreat into himself during break times, becoming almost invisible. Manuel tried to explain his struggles, but each attempt left him frustrated and tongue-tied, unable to articulate the chaos swirling in his mind. The words felt trapped, fraying at the edges like the very memories he wished to escape. Isolated by his pain, Manuel’s avoidance strategies grew ever more entrenched. He found solace in silence, often opting to stay home rather than risk the unpredictable world outside. He believed he was doing the right thing by avoiding triggers, convinced that any confrontation with his memories would bring only further harm. "The persistent reminders of his traumatic past made him increasingly reluctant to venture outside, leading him to avoid social gatherings and even his welding shop, convinced that any unexpected sound could trigger another wave of panic." Yet with each passing day spent inside, the walls of his home echoed with the haunting sounds of gunfire and screams, reinforcing his belief that the external world was filled with threats he could not escape. "His conviction that the world was a dangerous place meant that even minor reminders of his trauma would lead him to retreat further into isolation, avoiding life outside his home to stave off feelings of vulnerability." "Believing that the world was fraught with danger and that he had no control over his surroundings, Manuel found himself choosing to stay home more often, as it seemed the only sensible way to protect himself from the threats he imagined lurked outside." Yet this self-imposed exile only deepened the cycle of fear and regret. "Each time he heard the clanging of metal at the shop, he felt an overwhelming urge to retreat, believing that avoiding the shop altogether would shield him from the memories that threatened to engulf him." His conviction that he could never truly know who might betray or harm him again made him avoid social situations altogether, as he was convinced that facing others would only amplify his anxiety and fears. The walls of his home echoed with the haunting sounds of gunfire and screams, reverberating through his thoughts, reinforcing his belief that the world was a dangerous place. Finally, after years of suffering in silence, something shifted within Manuel. A moment of clarity came to him as he sat alone, grappling with the weight of his memories. He realized that he could no longer bear the burden alone. The thought of continuing to live in fear, to let the trauma dictate his every move, was unbearable. He hoped to find a way to untangle the threads of his past and reclaim a sense of safety in his life. As he contemplated reaching out for help, he was filled with a mix of hope and fear, terrified of confronting the truths he had buried but equally terrified of remaining trapped in his pain. "This belief that he was powerless in the face of trauma heightened his sensitivity to the world around him, causing even benign situations to feel fraught with danger and confirming his fears whenever he heard loud noises." "The vividness of the memories made him hyperaware of his surroundings, where every loud noise or sudden movement would send him spiraling into a state of distress, as if he were once again trapped in that dark room." "This heightened sense of danger led him to avoid crowded places and social interactions, convinced that any unexpected noise could trigger another wave of panic he couldn't handle." "This pervasive doubt about others' intentions led him to avoid making new connections or deepening existing ones, fearing that any relationship could turn sour and expose him to more emotional pain." "His conviction that he was powerless heightened his sensitivity to the sounds around him, making even ordinary clanging evoke memories of violence that he felt he could never escape." "This constant state of alertness led him to avoid situations where he might encounter unexpected noises, such as leaving the welding shop early whenever he sensed an incoming storm, convinced that the thunder would echo the gunfire from his past." "This belief that he was powerless in the face of trauma heightened his sensitivity to the world around him, causing even benign situations to feel fraught with danger and confirming his fears whenever he heard loud noises." "The intrusive memories made him hyper-aware of his surroundings, leading him to avoid certain streets and areas that reminded him of his past, convinced that any familiar sound could trigger another panic attack." "This belief left him feeling trapped, leading him to withdraw from social interactions altogether, as he felt that expressing his emotions would only expose him to more pain and judgment." "Each time a loud noise broke the silence, it felt like a confirmation of his worst fears, sending him spiraling into distress and prompting him to avoid any situation where he might encounter unexpected sounds."

  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."

  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."

  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."

  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Manuel, a 70-year-old widowed welder from Latin America, sat in his cluttered living room, the shadows lengthening as evening approached. His hands, calloused from years of labor, trembled slightly as he recalled a time that haunted him. It was decades ago, during a tumultuous period of political unrest in his home country, when he was captured and tortured by government forces. The memories were not distant; they felt present, as if the terror was happening again in that very moment. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a car door slamming, a sudden shout from a neighbor — felt like warnings he couldn't afford to ignore, and he found himself bracing for danger in moments that should have felt safe. "Because the memory came back so vividly, he began to see threads of it everywhere: in the shadow of passing cars, in the way people raised their voices during arguments, and in the tension of the air before a storm." Gunshots, echoing in the distance, triggered visceral reactions in him that no amount of time could diminish. Each crack of a firearm sent waves of panic coursing through his body, transporting him back to the dark, oppressive room where he had been held. In moments of distress, Manuel found himself trapped in a cycle of detachment. He would often try to push the memories away, suppressing the thoughts of his past as if they were mere shadows. Yet, the harder he fought to forget, the more vivid the memories became, erupting into his consciousness with an intensity that left him gasping for air, filled with rage at his helplessness. He had come to believe that this rage, this intense feeling boiling within him, was an unending reminder of his failure to protect himself and others during that horrific time. The conclusion that he was powerless in the face of such trauma led him to withdraw further from those around him, believing that isolating himself was the only rational choice to avoid potential harm. The guilt gnawed at him, leading him to think that he could have done more, that perhaps if he had fought harder, he could have changed the course of those dark days. The self-blame became suffocating, reinforcing his fear of the world around him. He felt that he could never truly know who might betray or harm him again, and this belief made him overly compliant in interactions, as if by pleasing others, he could somehow stave off danger. The weight of his past loomed heavily over his present. Every time he heard the clanging of metal at the welding shop, he was reminded of his past traumas, which only confirmed his belief that the world was a dangerous place and that he had no control over his surroundings. When he ventured out to the welding shop, the sounds of machinery often morphed into echoes of his trauma, the clanging metal reminding him too much of the violence he had endured. His colleagues noticed his abrupt withdrawal, how he would flinch at loud noises and retreat into himself during break times, becoming almost invisible. Manuel tried to explain his struggles, but each attempt left him frustrated and tongue-tied, unable to articulate the chaos swirling in his mind. The words felt trapped, fraying at the edges like the very memories he wished to escape. Isolated by his pain, Manuel’s avoidance strategies grew ever more entrenched. He found solace in silence, often opting to stay home rather than risk the unpredictable world outside. He believed he was doing the right thing by avoiding triggers, convinced that any confrontation with his memories would bring only further harm. "The persistent reminders of his traumatic past made him increasingly reluctant to venture outside, leading him to avoid social gatherings and even his welding shop, convinced that any unexpected sound could trigger another wave of panic."
